hops.title: Say it: worms breathe through their skin
hops.text: Try saying, "A worm breathes through its skin, so damp dirt is part of its home." Earthworms have no lungs and breathe right through their moist skin, so they need soil that stays damp. Save the line for when your child insists plain dirt cannot be part of a habitat.

sources.citation: Washington State University Insider, Ask Dr. Universe, "Dr. Universe explains why worms come out when it rains"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A pink earthworm coming out of dark, damp soil next to green clover leaves and small water droplets.
image.caption: An earthworm breathes through its damp skin, so moist soil is part of its habitat.

hops.title: Compare it: two wet sponges and the pill bugs
hops.text: If you rolled a log, gently roll it back first. Then wet two matching sponges with the same amount of water. Set one on a sunny outdoor table and cover the other with an upside-down bowl. Squeeze both later. Pill bugs are crustaceans, not insects, and they dry out easily. They curl into a ball to hold in water.

sources.citation: University of Kentucky Department of Entomology, ENTFACT-439, Olivia Katz, Zachary DeVries and Jonathan Larson, "Sowbugs and Pillbugs (aka Rolly-Pollies)"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two kitchen sponges on an outdoor table, one in the sun and one under a bowl, with a pill bug on damp soil by a log.
image.caption: Like a sponge in the shade, a pill bug stays damp in the cool shelter under a log.

hops.title: Point at it: a mowed lawn beside a clover patch
hops.text: When you pass a closely mowed yard beside a taller, clover-dotted patch, keep your child close and stay a step back to watch the bees without touching. In a Forest Service study, lawns mowed every three weeks had about 2.5 times as many lawn flowers as weekly-mowed ones. Lawns mowed every two weeks had the most bees, but fewer kinds.

sources.citation: Lerman, Contosta, Milam and Bang (2018), "To mow or to mow less: Lawn mowing frequency affects bee abundance and diversity in suburban yards", Biological Conservation (USDA Forest Service Treesearch)
University of Massachusetts Amherst News (March 13, 2018), "'Lazy Lawn Mowers' Can Help Support Suburban Bee Populations and Diversity"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Short mowed grass beside a taller patch with white clover, dandelions and two bumblebees, with a parent and child watching from the sidewalk.
image.caption: Clover and dandelion flowers give bees food. Watch from a step back.

audio.title: Three playful ways to talk about backyard habitats
audio.transcript: Here are three playful ways to help the habitat idea click while you are outside together. First, the worm line. If your child looks at plain brown dirt and says it cannot be part of anyone's home, try saying, "A worm breathes through its skin, so damp dirt is part of its home." Earthworms have no lungs at all. They breathe right through their moist skin, and they need soil about as damp as a wrung-out sponge. Suddenly the mud matters. Second, the sponge test. If you looked under a log, gently roll it back while your child stands back. Then wet two matching kitchen sponges with the same amount of water and set them on a sunny outdoor table. Cover one with an upside-down bowl. Later in the day, let your child squeeze both. Pill bugs are crustaceans, not insects, and they dry out easily. They even curl into a tight ball to hold in water. That is why the log goes back. Third, the bee patch. On a walk, find a short, freshly mowed lawn next to a taller patch full of clover and dandelions. Keep your child close, stay a step back, and watch the bees without touching them. Forest Service researchers and their colleagues studied sixteen yards. Lawns mowed every three weeks had about two and a half times as many lawn flowers as lawns mowed every week. Lawns mowed every two weeks had the most bees, but fewer kinds of bees. Ask your child which patch looks like a better place to be a bee, and let them tell you why. Happy hunting.
